title: Naked Mole Rats: A Face Only a Mother Could Love
summary: Josh and Chuck explore naked mole rats as part of the Amazing Animals edition: their taxonomy (family Bathyergidae, genus Heterocephalus), Horn of Africa habitat, fossorial lifestyle, teeth used as tools and sense organs, jaw musculature, conveyor-belt digging, low-oxygen tolerance via fructose metabolism, eusocial colony structure with a breeding queen, inbreeding, coprophagy and microbiota transfer, water from tubers, thermoregulation, extreme longevity and resistance to cancer and aging linked to high molecular weight hyaluronan, and reduced pain sensitivity. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about the origin of the Georgetown Hoya nickname.
topics: Fast, Cheap and Out of Control

entities.name: Fast, Cheap and Out of Control

segments.title: Opening and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Amazing Animals edition and naked mole rats as the episode pick, with Chuck recalling the Errol Morris documentary Fast, Cheap and Out of Control.
topics: Fast, Cheap and Out of Control

segments.title: Taxonomy and naming
segments.summary: Naked mole rats were first described by Edward Rüppell in 1842 and were doubted by other biologists. They are rodents in family Bathyergidae and genus Heterocephalus, and some researchers propose their own family.

segments.title: Habitat, appearance and fossorial life
segments.summary: Naked mole rats live in arid Horn of Africa countries including Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia, are not threatened, and spend their lives underground. They have poor eyesight, almost no ears, and are about three to four inches long; they diverged from guinea pigs about fifty million years ago.

segments.title: Teeth and jaw muscles
segments.summary: Incisors grow outside the mouth so the mouth can close while digging, and a large part of the somatosensory cortex serves the teeth. Jaw muscles make up about a quarter of body muscle mass.

segments.title: Digging and conveyor-belt tunneling
segments.summary: Colony members dig tunnels in a conveyor-belt system, with workers sweeping dirt back and a larger mole rat kicking it out to form molehills. They have sparse hair and sensory whiskers.

segments.title: Tunnel systems and movement
segments.summary: Tunnel systems can span miles across about five acres, and colonies crawl over one another. Naked mole rats move backward as fast as forward.

segments.title: Low oxygen tolerance and fructose metabolism
segments.summary: Colonies of 70 to 300 mole rats survive in low-oxygen, high-carbon-dioxide burrows, using a fructose metabolic pathway in the brain that works without oxygen. They tolerate five percent oxygen for at least five hours.

segments.title: Queen dominance and inbreeding
segments.summary: The queen shoves workers and suppresses reproduction in other colony members, who mature sexually when removed from the colony. Colonies are highly inbred, with the queen and her offspring genetically similar at about 0.8.

segments.title: Genetic similarity and lifespan
segments.summary: Genetic similarity figures are discussed: any two colony members about 0.5, and identical twins 1.0. Captive naked mole rats live about 30 to 40 years, far longer than mice.

segments.title: Thermoregulation and humidity
segments.summary: Naked mole rats are effectively cold-blooded through behavioral thermoregulation. Tunnels stay around the eighties Fahrenheit with 50 to 60 percent humidity.

segments.title: Water sourcing, tuber feeding, and coprophagy
segments.summary: They get water from roots, bulbs, rhizomes and tubers, sometimes regenerating large tubers. They eat their own and others' feces, which recycles undigested food and transfers gut microbiota and estrogen cues to pups. The queen sings a toilet song.

segments.title: Eusociality and colony structure
segments.summary: Naked mole rats are the only known eusocial mammals, with castes and a breeding queen; the discovery came through Richard Alexander's hypothetical description and Jennifer Jarvis's recognition. Queens fight to succeed, grow longer spines, and colonies sometimes split like bee swarms.

segments.title: Aging, cancer resistance and hyaluronan
segments.summary: Naked mole rats show little sign of aging and resist tumors. High molecular weight hyaluronan is implicated, found in their skin in higher amounts and larger molecules; it was transferred to mice to improve health. Their loose skin is linked to this molecule.

segments.title: Pain insensitivity
segments.summary: Naked mole rats have a high pain threshold and their skin does not respond to acid or capsaicin. Their nervous system seems to provide just enough pain signaling to survive.

segments.title: Closing remarks on naked mole rats
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up with a recommendation to watch Smithsonian naked mole rat videos and Fast, Cheap and Out of Control, which profiles Ray Mendez, a naked mole rat scientist.

segments.title: Listener mail: Georgetown Hoya nickname
segments.summary: Listener Mark Meyer explains that Georgetown's Hoya nickname derives from a Latin cheer, Hoya Saxa, referring to the stone walls, which is why students answer What is a Hoya with exactly.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener mail and close the show.
